title: Chaperone the Zoo Trip
text:
In 1975 Robert Cialdini and his colleagues at Arizona State University sent researchers across campus to stop students and ask a large favor. Would they volunteer as unpaid counselors for juvenile offenders, two hours a week, for at least two years? Every single student refused.

Right after the refusal, the researcher made a second, much smaller request: would they instead chaperone a group of juveniles on a two-hour trip to the zoo? Half of these students agreed. When other students were asked only about the zoo trip, with no big request first, about one in six said yes.

Cialdini called this the door-in-the-face technique and explained it as a matter of reciprocal concessions. When the asker retreated from the huge request to a modest one, it felt like a concession, and people tend to answer a concession with one of their own. In a control condition where the two options were simply described together, without a visible retreat, the effect was much weaker. The key was not the contrast in size alone, but the feeling that the other person had given ground.
lesson: People answer concessions with concessions. In a negotiation, notice when a retreat is staged to pull a yes from you, and remember that giving ground yourself can open the other side.
people: Robert Cialdini, Joyce Vincent, Stephen Lewis, Jose Catalan, Diane Wheeler, Betty Lee Darby
source: Cialdini, R. B., Vincent, J. E., Lewis, S. K., Catalan, J., Wheeler, D., and Darby, B. L. (1975). Reciprocal concessions procedure for inducing compliance: The door-in-the-face technique. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 31(2), 206-215.
